verses.text: Now as touching things offered unto idols, we know that we all have knowledge. Knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth.
And if any man think that he knoweth any thing, he knoweth nothing yet as he ought to know.
But if any man love God, the same is known of him.
As concerning therefore the eating of those things that are offered in sacrifice unto idols, we know that an idol is nothing in the world, and that there is none other God but one.
For though there be that are called gods, whether in heaven or in earth, ( as there be gods many, and lords many,)
But to us there is but one God, the Father, of whom are all things, and we in him; and one Lord Jesus Christ, by whom are all things, and we by him.
Howbeit there is not in every man that knowledge: for some with conscience of the idol unto this hour eat it as a thing offered unto an idol; and their conscience being weak is defiled.
But meat commendeth us not to God: for neither, if we eat, are we the better; neither, if we eat not, are we the worse.
But take heed lest by any means this liberty of yours become a stumblingblock to them that are weak.
For if any man see thee which hast knowledge sit at meat in the idol’s temple, shall not the conscience of him which is weak be emboldened to eat those things which are offered to idols;
And through thy knowledge shall the weak brother perish, for whom Christ died?
But when ye sin so against the brethren, and wound their weak conscience, ye sin against Christ.
Wherefore, if meat make my brother to offend, I will eat no flesh while the world standeth, lest I make my brother to offend.

summary: The Corinthians had written to Paul about food that had passed through a pagan altar before it reached the market or the banquet hall, and he answers by first refusing the terms of the question. "Now as touching things offered unto idols, we know that we all have knowledge" concedes their premise and in the same breath puts it under judgment: "Knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth." The measure of maturity is then inverted, since "if any man think that he knoweth any thing, he knoweth nothing yet as he ought to know," and the decisive relation turns out not to be our grasp of God but his of us: "if any man love God, the same is known of him." Only after that reordering does Paul grant the argument on its own ground. "An idol is nothing in the world, and ... there is none other God but one"; though the city is crowded with "gods many, and lords many," the confession of the church is single and yet twofold in its naming — "to us there is but one God, the Father, of whom are all things, and we in him; and one Lord Jesus Christ, by whom are all things, and we by him." Having conceded the theology, he denies the conclusion drawn from it. "Howbeit there is not in every man that knowledge": some believers still eat "with conscience of the idol unto this hour," and "their conscience being weak is defiled." The food itself settles nothing — "meat commendeth us not to God: for neither, if we eat, are we the better; neither, if we eat not, are we the worse" — which is exactly why the enlightened eater has so little to gain and the weak brother so much to lose. "But take heed lest by any means this liberty of yours become a stumblingblock to them that are weak." The case Paul imagines is concrete: a man "which hast knowledge" is seen "sit at meat in the idol’s temple," a weaker conscience is "emboldened" to imitate him against its own judgment, "and through thy knowledge shall the weak brother perish, for whom Christ died?" The injury then travels past the brother to the Lord himself: "when ye sin so against the brethren, and wound their weak conscience, ye sin against Christ." Paul ends not with a regulation imposed on others but with a vow taken on himself, unlimited in scope and voluntary in kind: "if meat make my brother to offend, I will eat no flesh while the world standeth, lest I make my brother to offend."
takeaways: Paul does not answer the knowledge question by supplying better knowledge. He relocates it. "Knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth" sets two verbs against each other — one inflates a single person, the other builds a structure that houses many — and the sentence that follows refuses to let anyone claim the higher ground: "if any man think that he knoweth any thing, he knoweth nothing yet as he ought to know." The way out is not more information but a different posture, and even there Paul breaks the expected symmetry. The line should end "but if any man love God, the same knoweth him." Instead it reads "the same is known of him." What finally matters is not the size of our grasp on God but that we are held.

The confession in verse six is one of the earliest and densest statements of Christian faith anywhere in the letters, and it is dropped almost casually into an argument about dinner. Against a world of "gods many, and lords many," Paul writes "to us there is but one God, the Father, of whom are all things, and we in him; and one Lord Jesus Christ, by whom are all things, and we by him." The oneness of God is not diluted by the two names; rather the same universal scope — "all things" — is predicated of the Father as source and of Christ as agent, and the believers' own existence is located in both. A Jewish monotheist has reworked the ancestral confession around Jesus without conceding a second deity.

Correct doctrine turns out to be insufficient by itself, and can even be the instrument of the harm. Everything the strong Corinthians believe is true — "an idol is nothing in the world" — and Paul says so plainly. Yet the same paragraph adds "Howbeit there is not in every man that knowledge," and the damage in the chapter is done entirely by people who are right. Truth held without reference to the person seated beside you becomes a way of winning rather than a way of loving, which is what makes "knowledge puffeth up" a diagnosis and not an insult.

The neutrality of the disputed thing is what makes the demand reasonable rather than harsh. Because "meat commendeth us not to God: for neither, if we eat, are we the better; neither, if we eat not, are we the worse," nothing spiritual is forfeited by abstaining. The risk is entirely one-sided: the strong lose a meal, while the weak conscience is "defiled" and may "perish." Once the stakes are seen to be that unequal, insisting on the right becomes hard to describe as anything but self-assertion, and Paul names the outcome bluntly — "this liberty of yours" has become "a stumblingblock to them that are weak."

The worth of the weak brother is fixed by the cross, not by his level of understanding. Paul could have said the confused convert should be taught better, and elsewhere he does teach; here he says instead "through thy knowledge shall the weak brother perish, for whom Christ died." The valuation is external to the man's competence and equal to the Lord's own outlay. That is what allows the next sentence to escalate the offense past the community: "when ye sin so against the brethren, and wound their weak conscience, ye sin against Christ." The wound is located in the conscience rather than the appetite, which means the sin is against a person's integrity before God.

The chapter closes with a vow rather than a rule, and the difference is deliberate. "Wherefore, if meat make my brother to offend, I will eat no flesh while the world standeth, lest I make my brother to offend" is first person, permanent in reach, and imposed on nobody. Paul binds himself more severely than he asks anyone else to be bound, and he does it in the one area where he has just proved he is free. Freedom is not surrendered as a principle; it is spent, which is the only thing freedom is finally for.

crossRefs.label: Romans 14:15,20 — Destroy not him with thy meat, for whom Christ died
crossRefs.why: Paul works the identical problem for a different community, and the shared phrase "for whom Christ died" shows the reasoning is not local to Corinth. There the neutral thing is diet and days rather than sacrificial meat, and the same two moves appear: the strong are told they are right, and then told that being right is not the question. Reading the two together separates the doctrine of liberty from the pastoral use of it.

crossRefs.label: 1 Corinthians 10:23-24 — All things are lawful for me, but all things edify not
crossRefs.why: Two chapters later Paul returns to the same meat with an added warning: idols are nothing, yet what pagans sacrifice has a real spiritual character, and "ye cannot be partakers of the Lord’s table, and of the table of devils." The pairing keeps chapter eight from being read as pure permissiveness, and supplies the practical rule the earlier chapter withholds — buy what is sold, ask no questions, but stop the moment someone else's conscience is engaged.

crossRefs.label: Deuteronomy 6:4-5 — Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God is one LORD
crossRefs.why: Verse six is a Christian rewriting of Israel's central confession, keeping the insistence on one God while distributing the ancient words across the Father and "one Lord Jesus Christ." The original text binds the confession to love — "thou shalt love the LORD thy God" — which is exactly the note Paul strikes before he ever gets to monotheism, when he writes "if any man love God, the same is known of him."

crossRefs.label: Matthew 18:6 — whoso shall offend one of these little ones... it were better for him that a millstone were hanged about his neck
crossRefs.why: The Lord's warning about causing a little one to stumble stands behind Paul's language of a "stumblingblock" and of making "my brother to offend." Both treat the weaker party as the one whose safety governs the stronger party's freedom, and both attach an extraordinary penalty to the one who trades another's soul for his own convenience.

crossRefs.label: 1 Corinthians 13:2,8 — though I... understand all mysteries, and all knowledge... and have not charity, I am nothing
crossRefs.why: The hymn to charity is the full development of the sentence that opens this chapter. "Knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth" becomes the extended judgment that knowledge "shall vanish away" while charity "never faileth," and the ironic reversal is preserved: the man with all knowledge and no love "is nothing," the same word Paul uses here for an idol.

crossRefs.label: Acts 15:28-29 — that ye abstain from meats offered to idols... from things strangled
crossRefs.why: The apostolic assembly at Jerusalem had already issued a common decision on this exact food, phrased as a burden deliberately kept light and issued with the words "it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us." Catholic reading gives this precedent real weight, since it shows the apostolic Church settling a disputed matter of practice by a shared, binding judgment rather than leaving each conscience to itself — the corporate counterpart to the personal restraint Paul urges here.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading treats scandal in this chapter as a true moral category with public consequences, not merely a failure of tact. To "sin so against the brethren, and wound their weak conscience" is to "sin against Christ," so leading another to act against his own conscience is itself sinful, and the Church is understood to have real competence to regulate things that are indifferent in themselves — days of abstinence, fasting discipline, customs of practice — precisely because the good of the whole body and the protection of the weak can require it. The tradition also notes that a weak conscience is a condition to be healed rather than indefinitely humored: conscience must always be obeyed, but it must also be formed, and Paul's forbearance buys time for the instruction that follows rather than replacing it.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters agree fully that scandal is real sin and that the strong owe the weak restraint, but they resist the step from Paul's counsel to churchwide law. They observe that the chapter's only actual commitment is first person and voluntary — "I will eat no flesh while the world standeth" — that Paul never withdraws his verdict that "meat commendeth us not to God," and that he refuses to issue the rule the Corinthians probably wanted. On this reading, converting charity's self-limitation into required observance in matters Scripture leaves open re-imposes on conscience the very bondage the chapter dissolves, and can entrench the weakness rather than heal it. Both traditions hold that in the concrete case love, not liberty, decides.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading takes "there is none other God but one" as excluding from every creature the adoration owed to God alone, while not excluding honour given to creatures whom God has glorified. The sin Paul condemns is directing worship to what he has just called a nothing — "an idol is nothing in the world" — whereas the saints and angels are not nothings but living members of the body of the "one Lord Jesus Christ," so that asking their prayer is understood as an act within the household of the one God rather than a rival to him. The tradition also reads verse six as guarding rather than dividing that oneness, since "all things" are predicated of the Father as source and of Christ as agent without producing two gods.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant readings hear the confession as drawing a sharper and more exclusive line. Set against a culture of "gods many, and lords many," the assertion that "to us there is but one God, the Father" and "one Lord Jesus Christ" is taken to concentrate all religious address on God alone, and many hold that devotion offered to any creature — even honour carefully distinguished from adoration — blurs a boundary this chapter draws hard, particularly given the warning about two tables that follows two chapters later. The only mediating figures Paul names are the Father from whom all things come and the Lord by whom they come. Both traditions affirm that the verse is an unqualified confession of one God and that it places Christ on the divine side of that confession.

interpretationNotes.claim: In the Catholic reading, the opening contrast bears directly on how a person is actually joined to God. "Knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth," followed by "if any man think that he knoweth any thing, he knoweth nothing yet as he ought to know," is heard as denying that correct assent by itself constitutes the saving relation; the pivot is love — "if any man love God, the same is known of him." This supports the conviction that faith is completed and given its living form by charity, so that a faith without charity is not merely unproductive but unfinished, and that the theological virtues are ordered with love as the greatest.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters read the contrast as pastoral rather than as a statement about the instrument of justification. Paul is puncturing a particular Corinthian arrogance about idol meat, not adjudicating how a sinner is accounted righteous. On this reading, the knowledge he dismisses is bare notional assent, which was never what is meant by saving faith; genuine trust in Christ is living and necessarily issues in love, so charity is the inseparable fruit and evidence of faith rather than an added component that completes it. Both traditions agree with Paul's actual verdict, that knowledge which fails to build up the brother has misunderstood what knowing is for.

authoring.attributionNotes: Original synthesis grounded in the KJV text and the general Catholic/Christian interpretive tradition. No specific published source is quoted or cited; tradition labels denote a position, not a copied source.
